[2020 summer phd probability — problem 2]

A population in which each individual is at any time in one of three states $A$, $B$, $C$ evolves in discrete time: (1) each individual in state $A$ in generation $n$ produces a random number $\xi_x$ of offspring in generation $n+1$, all of type $B$, then dies, where $P(\xi_x = k) = \alpha^k(1-\alpha)$, $k = 0,1,2,\dots$, for $0 < \alpha < 1$; (2) each individual in state $B$ in generation $n$ mutates to state $A$ with probability $p$ or to state $C$ with probability $q = 1-p$ ($0 < p < 1$); (3) each individual in state $C$ dies; (4) all individuals act independently. Let $Z^i_n$ be the number of individuals in state $i$ in generation $n$; assume $Z^A_0 = 1$ (a single individual in state $A$ at time $0$).
(a) Show that with probability $1$, either $Z^A_n = Z^B_n = Z^C_n = 0$ for all large $n$, or $\lim_{n\to\infty}(Z^A_n + Z^B_n + Z^C_n) = \infty$.
(b) Express $\mathbb{E}(Z^A_n)$, $\mathbb{E}(Z^B_n)$ and $\mathbb{E}(Z^C_n)$ as functions of $\alpha$, $p$ and $n$.
(c) Let $p_e = P(Z^A_n = Z^B_n = Z^C_n = 0 \text{ for all large } n)$ be the extinction probability. For which values of $\alpha$ and $p$ is $p_e = 1$? Give a proof.
(d) In the case $p_e < 1$, find an explicit closed-form expression for $p_e$ in terms of $\alpha$ and $p$.
(e) Define sequences $\{a(n)\}_{n\ge1}$ and $\{b(n)\}_{n\ge1}$ such that $Y_n := Z^B_{a(n)}/b(n)$ converges almost surely to a finite limiting random variable. Give explicit forms of $a(n), b(n)$ and prove the convergence.

## Preliminary reduction to a one-type Galton–Watson process

Let

\[
m:=\mathbb E \xi=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha},\qquad q=1-p,\qquad 
\mu:=mp=\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}.
\]

Because we start with one type \(A\) individual at time \(0\), the process has period \(2\):

\[
Z^A_{2n+1}=0,\qquad Z^B_{2n}=0,\qquad Z^C_{2n+1}=0.
\]

Define the embedded process

\[
X_n:=Z^A_{2n},\qquad n\ge 0.
\]

A type \(A\) individual at time \(2n\) produces \(\xi\) type \(B\) individuals at time \(2n+1\). Each of those independently becomes type \(A\) with probability \(p\). Thus the number \(\eta\) of type \(A\) grandchildren two generations later has pgf

\[
f(s):=\mathbb E(s^\eta)
=\mathbb E\bigl[(q+ps)^\xi\bigr]
=\sum_{k=0}^\infty (1-\alpha)\alpha^k(q+ps)^k
=\frac{1-\alpha}{1-\alpha q-\alpha p s}.
\]

Therefore \(\{X_n\}_{n\ge 0}\) is a one-type Galton–Watson process with offspring pgf \(f\) and mean

\[
f'(1)=\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}=\mu.
\]

Also,

\[
\{Z^A_n=Z^B_n=Z^C_n=0\text{ for all large }n\}
=
\{X_n=0\text{ for some }n\}.
\]

Indeed, if \(X_n=0\), then no type \(A\) individuals remain at time \(2n\), so no type \(B\) individuals appear at time \(2n+1\), and any type \(C\) individuals present die. Conversely, eventual extinction clearly implies \(X_n=0\) eventually.

---

## (a) Extinction-or-explosion dichotomy

Let

\[
N_n:=Z^A_n+Z^B_n+Z^C_n.
\]

The embedded process \(X_n=Z^A_{2n}\) is a Galton–Watson process.

By the standard Galton–Watson theorem, if \(X_n\) becomes extinct, then the whole population becomes extinct after finitely many generations. That gives the first alternative.

On the nonextinction event, the Galton–Watson process \(X_n\) survives forever. For a supercritical Galton–Watson process, conditional on nonextinction,

\[
X_n\to\infty \qquad \text{a.s.}
\]

One way to prove this is to note that if the process visited a finite set \(\{1,\dots,K\}\) infinitely often, then at each such visit it would have a uniformly positive conditional probability of eventual extinction, contradicting survival.

Thus on nonextinction,

\[
Z^A_{2n}=X_n\to\infty.
\]

Hence

\[
N_{2n}\ge Z^A_{2n}=X_n\to\infty.
\]

Also every type \(A\) individual at time \(2n+2\) must have arisen from a type \(B\) individual at time \(2n+1\). Therefore

\[
Z^B_{2n+1}\ge Z^A_{2n+2}=X_{n+1}.
\]

So on nonextinction,

\[
N_{2n+1}=Z^B_{2n+1}\ge X_{n+1}\to\infty.
\]

Combining the even and odd subsequences,

\[
N_n\to\infty
\]

on the nonextinction event. Hence with probability \(1\), either the population is eventually extinct or its total size tends to infinity.

---

## (b) Expectations

Let

\[
a_n:=\mathbb E Z^A_n,\qquad b_n:=\mathbb E Z^B_n,\qquad c_n:=\mathbb E Z^C_n.
\]

The recursions are

\[
a_{n+1}=p b_n,\qquad b_{n+1}=m a_n,\qquad c_{n+1}=q b_n,
\]

with

\[
a_0=1,\qquad b_0=c_0=0.
\]

Since \(\mu=mp=\dfrac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}\), we obtain

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E Z^A_{2r}=\mu^r,\qquad \mathbb E Z^A_{2r+1}=0.}
\]

Also,

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E Z^B_{2r+1}=m\mu^r
=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\left(\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}\right)^r,\qquad 
\mathbb E Z^B_{2r}=0.}
\]

Finally, for \(r\ge 1\),

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E Z^C_{2r}=q m\mu^{r-1}
=(1-p)\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}
\left(\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}\right)^{r-1},}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E Z^C_{2r+1}=0,\qquad \mathbb E Z^C_0=0.}
\]

---

## (c) Values of \(\alpha,p\) for which \(p_e=1\)

The extinction probability \(p_e\) is the extinction probability of the embedded Galton–Watson process \(X_n\). Its mean offspring number is

\[
\mu=\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}.
\]

By the Galton–Watson extinction theorem, extinction occurs almost surely if and only if \(\mu\le 1\). Therefore

\[
p_e=1
\iff \frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}\le 1
\iff \alpha p\le 1-\alpha
\iff \alpha(1+p)\le 1.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{p_e=1 \iff \alpha\le \frac{1}{1+p}.}
\]

Equivalently, survival has positive probability precisely when

\[
\boxed{\alpha>\frac{1}{1+p}.}
\]

---

## (d) Closed form for \(p_e\) when \(p_e<1\)

When \(p_e<1\), the embedded Galton–Watson process is supercritical, so

\[
\mu=\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}>1.
\]

The extinction probability is the smallest solution in \([0,1]\) of

\[
s=f(s)=\frac{1-\alpha}{1-\alpha q-\alpha p s}.
\]

Thus

\[
s(1-\alpha q-\alpha p s)=1-\alpha.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\alpha p s^2-(1-\alpha q)s+(1-\alpha)=0.
\]

The two roots are

\[
s=1
\]

and

\[
s=\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha p}.
\]

In the supercritical case,

\[
\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha p}<1,
\]

so the extinction probability is the smaller root:

\[
\boxed{p_e=\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha p}.}
\]

---

## (e) Almost sure normalization of \(Z^B_n\)

A natural nontrivial subsequence is the odd generations, since \(Z^B_{2n}=0\). Define

\[
\boxed{a(n)=2n-1}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
b(n)=\mathbb E Z^B_{2n-1}
=m\mu^{n-1}
=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}
\left(\frac{\alpha p}{1-\alpha}\right)^{n-1}.
}
\]

We show that

\[
Y_n:=\frac{Z^B_{2n-1}}{b(n)}
\]

converges almost surely to a finite random variable.

Assume first the supercritical case \(\mu>1\). Let

\[
X_n=Z^A_{2n}.
\]

Then

\[
M_n:=\frac{X_n}{\mu^n}
\]

is a nonnegative martingale with respect to the natural filtration, because

\[
\mathbb E[X_{n+1}\mid X_n]=\mu X_n.
\]

By Doob’s martingale convergence theorem,

\[
M_n\to W
\]

almost surely for some finite random variable \(W\).

Now condition on the population at time \(2n\). Given \(X_n\), the number of type \(B\) individuals at time \(2n+1\) is

\[
Z^B_{2n+1}=\sum_{j=1}^{X_n}\xi_{n,j},
\]

where the \(\xi_{n,j}\) are i.i.d. copies of \(\xi\). Since

\[
\mathbb E\xi=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\xi)=\frac{\alpha}{(1-\alpha)^2}<\infty,
\]

we have

\[
\mathbb E\left[
\left(
\frac{Z^B_{2n+1}-mX_n}{m\mu^n}
\right)^2
\right]
=
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\xi)\,\mathbb E X_n}{m^2\mu^{2n}}
=
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\xi)}{m^2}\mu^{-n}.
\]

Since \(\mu>1\),

\[
\sum_{n=0}^\infty 
\mathbb E\left[
\left(
\frac{Z^B_{2n+1}-mX_n}{m\mu^n}
\right)^2
\right]
<\infty.
\]

By Markov’s inequality and the Borel–Cantelli lemma,

\[
\frac{Z^B_{2n+1}-mX_n}{m\mu^n}\to 0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Therefore

\[
\frac{Z^B_{2n+1}}{m\mu^n}
=
\frac{X_n}{\mu^n}
+
\frac{Z^B_{2n+1}-mX_n}{m\mu^n}
\to W
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Replacing \(n\) by \(n-1\), we get

\[
\frac{Z^B_{2n-1}}{m\mu^{n-1}}\to W
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
Y_n=\frac{Z^B_{a(n)}}{b(n)}\to W
\qquad\text{a.s.}
}
\]

In the subcritical or critical case \(\mu\le 1\), part (c) shows extinction occurs almost surely, so \(Z^B_{2n-1}=0\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Hence then

\[
Y_n\to 0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Therefore the above choice of \(a(n)\) and \(b(n)\) gives almost sure convergence to a finite limiting random variable.
